question: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit to others or elevated the team rather than taking personal credit.

raiseTranscript.text: I was on a small feature team and we hit our deadline early. My manager asked me to present the demo, but I asked if the two engineers who fixed the tricky bugs could join and walk through their parts.
They explained the fixes, I highlighted how their changes unblocked the rest of the work, and the team got the recognition. I just summarized at the end.
Why did you do that instead of presenting yourself?
They did the hard parts and I wanted them to get the credit in front of the stakeholders.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit to others...
Role: new grad on 4-person feature team
Situation: demo request after early delivery
Action: asked two engineers to present their fixes, summarized at end
Outcome: team visibly credited in meeting
Quote: 'They did the hard parts and I wanted them to get the credit'
Follow-up: Why? 'Felt like the right thing and they deserved it.'
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Teamwork & Collaboration for junior level. Candidate described a small feature demo where they stepped back so two engineers could present their fixes instead of taking the spotlight. The concrete action was explicitly asking the manager to include the engineers and then only summarizing at the end. This shows early understanding that credit should flow to the people who did the work. At junior level we look for ownership of own actions and basic team orientation rather than heroics. The signal is clean and calibrated; the only gap is lack of scale, which is expected.

lowerTranscript.text: I finished the project ahead of schedule and my manager let me present it to leadership.
A couple people helped with reviews but I did most of the coding so I just mentioned them at the end.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit...
Candidate defaults to 'I finished the project'
Action: presented alone, mentioned reviewers briefly at end
Quote: 'I did most of the coding'
Follow-up: Why not have others present? No clear answer beyond 'it was my project'
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Teamwork & Collaboration for junior level. The candidate framed the win as their individual delivery and only mentioned reviewers at the very end when prompted. No evidence they actively elevated teammates or considered sharing the stage. At this level we expect at least basic recognition that work is rarely solo and willingness to share credit when asked. The story shows the opposite instinct.

raiseTranscript.text: We had a cross-team migration that was behind. I coordinated the plan but the actual cutover work came from two other teams. When leadership asked for the update I had the leads from those teams present their sections.
The other teams felt ownership and we got better adoption. I still owned the overall status but made sure their contributions were visible.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit...
Role: senior IC driving cross-team migration
Situation: behind schedule, multiple teams involved
Action: had owning team leads present their cutover work in leadership update
Outcome: higher ownership and adoption
Quote: 'I still owned the overall status but made sure their contributions were visible'
Follow-up: Did this slow you down? 'Slightly, but worth it for alignment.'
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Teamwork & Collaboration for senior level. Candidate described stepping back during a leadership update so the actual owning teams could present their cutover work rather than summarizing it themselves. The action directly influenced cross-team ownership and adoption. At senior level we expect influence without authority and deliberate elevation of partners. The story shows both the choice and the measurable team-level result.

lowerTranscript.text: I ran point on a big migration and got it done across three teams.
How did you handle updates with the other teams?
I gave them status and made sure leadership knew I was coordinating everything.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit...
Candidate centers self as 'ran point' and 'coordinating everything'
No mention of surfacing other teams' work in updates
Follow-up: How did other teams feel? 'They got the status they needed'
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Teamwork & Collaboration for senior level. The candidate consistently positions themselves as the central coordinator without describing any effort to make other teams' contributions visible. At senior level we expect cross-team influence and credit sharing as a tool for leverage; this example shows coordination without that orientation.

raiseTranscript.text: My team delivered a major platform upgrade. When the director asked who should present, I recommended two of my engineers who had driven the riskiest pieces and coached them on the deck.
What was the result for the team?
They got direct visibility with leadership and one later got promoted. I stayed in the room but let them own the narrative.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit...
Role: engineering manager
Situation: major platform upgrade ready for leadership review
Action: recommended two engineers to present, coached them on content
Outcome: direct visibility and one promotion
Quote: 'I stayed in the room but let them own the narrative'
Follow-up: Why not present yourself? 'They did the work and needed the exposure.'
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Teamwork & Collaboration for manager level. The candidate chose to give two engineers the leadership presentation slot on a platform upgrade and actively coached them. The outcome included a promotion for one of the engineers. At manager level we look for deliberate development of people through visibility and credit. The story ties the action to a concrete career result.

lowerTranscript.text: My team shipped the platform upgrade and I presented the results to the directors.
Did your team members get any exposure?
I mentioned a few names in the Q&A but I needed to represent the work accurately.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit...
Credit limited to name mentions in Q&A
Follow-up: Why not have team present? 'I needed to represent the work accurately'
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Teamwork & Collaboration for manager level. The manager took the presentation themselves and limited team visibility to name mentions during Q&A. At this level we expect managers to create leverage by developing and elevating their people; this example shows the opposite pattern of hoarding the spotlight.

raiseTranscript.text: After a company-wide reorg I had three orgs deliver a new infrastructure foundation. In the all-hands I had the three directors each present their org's contribution and only closed with the overall business impact.
The directors needed airtime with the broader leadership team and I wanted the organization to see this as a collective win, not something one exec delivered.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit...
Role: VP/Exec post-reorg
Situation: three orgs delivered shared infrastructure foundation
Action: had each director present their piece in all-hands
Outcome: visible collective ownership
Quote: 'I wanted the organization to see this as a collective win, not something one exec delivered'
Follow-up: Any pushback from peers? 'Some wanted one voice but I held the line.'
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Teamwork & Collaboration for exec level. The candidate structured a company all-hands so three directors presented their orgs' contributions instead of summarizing the work themselves. The explicit goal was signaling collective ownership after a reorg. At exec level we look for strategic use of visibility to shape culture and alignment across boundaries. The story shows both the mechanism and the intended organizational signal.

lowerTranscript.text: I led the reorg and the infrastructure program that followed and presented the results to the company.
How did you involve the org leaders?
They were in the room and I thanked them publicly at the end.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where you gave credit...
Candidate presented the full program themselves
Credit limited to public thanks at the end
Follow-up: Why not share the stage? No strategic rationale offered
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Teamwork & Collaboration for exec level. The candidate presented the reorg and infrastructure results themselves with only closing thanks to org leaders. At exec level we expect deliberate choices about who receives visibility to drive culture and leverage; this approach reinforces a single-leader narrative instead.
